## Study III: Clinical Dynamics (Simultaneous iEEG/EEG) {#sec-study3}

### Spatial Correlation Analysis

Study II scored a single location per patient. Study III instead tests how well each method reproduces the spatial pattern of activity recorded intracranially, across contacts and over time.

wCSET was compared against every other method at the timepoint level, on two sign-free measures: the amplitude rank correlation and the AUC (@sec-metric-corr, @sec-metric-auc), via the autocorrelation-corrected paired test of @sec-stats.

```{python filename="results_intra_vieeg_significance.py"}
#| output: false
import mindmap as mm
import pandas as pd

# Amplitude rank correlation (Spearman, |amplitude|) and AUC on |amplitude|, per subject, method and timepoint
# (processing_intra.qmd, "Spatial pattern metrics").
SPATIAL_DIR = "./results/intra/spatial_metrics"
vieeg_metrics = mm.metric.MetricSuite.load(SPATIAL_DIR)

# Subjects 12 and 50 (deep sources, far from the cortical source space) are reported in the Annex.
SUBJECT_ORDER = ["34", "48", "12", "50"]
MAIN_SUBJECTS = ["48", "34"]
SUBJECT_TITLES = {
    "34": "Subject 2",
    "48": "Subject 1",
    "12": "Subject 3\n(deep source)",
    "50": "Subject 4\n(deep source)",
}

# Competitor order matches processing_intra.qmd, whose cached statistics are reused.
COMPETITORS = ["sloreta", "cset", "dspm", "wmne", "beltrami"]
STANDARD = ["cset", "sloreta", "dspm", "wmne"]  # GBF reported separately
VIEEG_METRICS = {"correlation_spatial_absrank": "amplitude rank correlation", "auc_spatial": "AUC on |amplitude|"}

# Per-timepoint values and cached test results.
vieeg_wide, vieeg_results = {}, {}
for metric in VIEEG_METRICS:
    for subject in SUBJECT_ORDER:
        wide = (vieeg_metrics.to_df(metrics=metric, filters={"Subject": subject})
                .pivot_table(index="times", columns="Method", values="Value").dropna())
        vieeg_wide[(subject, metric)] = wide
        vieeg_results[(subject, metric)] = vieeg_metrics.stat.ttest_ess(
            metric, group_by="Method", comparisons=vieeg_metrics.stat.build_comparisons(["wcset"], COMPETITORS),
            pairing_col="times", subject_order=wide.index.tolist(), filters={"Subject": subject},
        )

# Statistics quoted in the prose: p-values and effects (positive = wCSET better) per competitor,
# and the per-timepoint differences wCSET - competitor behind each test.
vieeg_vs = {k: r.vs("wcset") for k, r in vieeg_results.items()}
vieeg_diffs = {k: vieeg_metrics.stat.paired_differences(r) for k, r in vieeg_results.items()}

def _median(subject, metric, method):
    return vieeg_wide[(subject, metric)][method].median()

_r, _auc = "correlation_spatial_absrank", "auc_spatial"

# Subject 1: wCSET vs. the four standard methods and CSET, then GBF.
_r48, _auc48 = vieeg_vs[("48", _r)], vieeg_vs[("48", _auc)]
_win48 = (vieeg_diffs[("48", _r)] > 0).mean() * 100  # % of timepoints where wCSET is higher
vieeg_48_r_wcset = fmt_num(_median("48", _r, "wcset"), 2)
vieeg_48_r_std_lo = fmt_num(min(_median("48", _r, c) for c in STANDARD), 2)
vieeg_48_r_std_hi = fmt_num(max(_median("48", _r, c) for c in STANDARD), 2)
vieeg_48_r_beltrami = fmt_num(_median("48", _r, "beltrami"), 2)
vieeg_48_spatial_p4_max = fmt_p(_r48.loc[STANDARD, "p_corrected"].max())
vieeg_48_spatial_dz4_lo = fmt_stat(_r48.loc[STANDARD, "effect"].min())
vieeg_48_spatial_dz4_hi = fmt_stat(_r48.loc[STANDARD, "effect"].max())
vieeg_48_winrate_min = f"{_win48[STANDARD].min():.0f}"
vieeg_48_winrate_max = f"{_win48[STANDARD].max():.0f}"
vieeg_48_spatial_p_beltrami = fmt_p(_r48.loc["beltrami", "p_corrected"])
vieeg_48_beltrami_winrate = f"{_win48['beltrami']:.0f}"
vieeg_48_auc_p4_max = fmt_p(_auc48.loc[STANDARD, "p_corrected"].max())
vieeg_48_auc_dz4_lo = fmt_stat(_auc48.loc[STANDARD, "effect"].min())
vieeg_48_auc_dz4_hi = fmt_stat(_auc48.loc[STANDARD, "effect"].max())
vieeg_48_auc_p_beltrami = fmt_p(_auc48.loc["beltrami", "p_corrected"])

# Subject 2: smallest p over every competitor and both metrics.
vieeg_34_p_min = fmt_p(min(vieeg_vs[("34", m)]["p_corrected"].min() for m in VIEEG_METRICS))
vieeg_34_r_wcset = fmt_num(_median("34", _r, "wcset"), 2)
vieeg_34_r_std_lo = fmt_num(min(_median("34", _r, c) for c in STANDARD), 2)
vieeg_34_r_std_hi = fmt_num(max(_median("34", _r, c) for c in STANDARD), 2)

# Signed Pearson correlation (Annex Figure 12), for comparison with Grova et al. 2016 and Afnan et al. 2026.
_signed = "correlation_spatial_signed"
_signed_vs, _signed_wide = {}, {}
for _s in MAIN_SUBJECTS:
    _w = (vieeg_metrics.to_df(metrics=_signed, filters={"Subject": _s})
          .pivot_table(index="times", columns="Method", values="Value").dropna())
    _signed_wide[_s] = _w
    _signed_vs[_s] = vieeg_metrics.stat.ttest_ess(
        _signed, group_by="Method", comparisons=vieeg_metrics.stat.build_comparisons(["wcset"], COMPETITORS),
        pairing_col="times", subject_order=_w.index.tolist(), filters={"Subject": _s},
    ).vs("wcset")
signed_48_wcset = fmt_num(_signed_wide["48"]["wcset"].median(), 2)
signed_48_std_lo = fmt_num(min(_signed_wide["48"][c].median() for c in STANDARD), 2)
signed_48_std_hi = fmt_num(max(_signed_wide["48"][c].median() for c in STANDARD), 2)
signed_48_p_max = fmt_p(_signed_vs["48"].loc[STANDARD, "p_corrected"].max())
signed_48_dz_lo = fmt_stat(_signed_vs["48"].loc[STANDARD, "effect"].min())
signed_48_dz_hi = fmt_stat(_signed_vs["48"].loc[STANDARD, "effect"].max())
signed_34_p_min = fmt_p(_signed_vs["34"]["p_corrected"].min())
signed_34_wcset = fmt_num(_signed_wide["34"]["wcset"].median(), 2)

# Glass-brain example (processing_intra.qmd): rho and top-contact overlap at the timepoint shown.
import json
_glass = {s_: json.load(open(f"./results/intra/glass_example/sub-{s_}.json")) for s_ in MAIN_SUBJECTS}
glass_n_top = _glass["48"]["n_top"]
glass_48_rho_wcset, glass_48_rho_sloreta = (fmt_num(_glass["48"]["rho"][m], 2) for m in ["wcset", "sloreta"])
glass_34_rho_wcset, glass_34_rho_sloreta = (fmt_num(_glass["34"]["rho"][m], 2) for m in ["wcset", "sloreta"])
glass_34_top_wcset, glass_34_top_sloreta = (_glass["34"]["top_overlap"][m] for m in ["wcset", "sloreta"])
```

In Subject 1 (@fig-intracranial-diff), wCSET's amplitude rank correlation with the recording (median ρ = `{python} vieeg_48_r_wcset`) was significantly higher than that of sLORETA, dSPM, wMNE and CSET (median ρ = `{python} vieeg_48_r_std_lo` to `{python} vieeg_48_r_std_hi`; largest p_corrected `{python} vieeg_48_spatial_p4_max`, dz = `{python} vieeg_48_spatial_dz4_lo`–`{python} vieeg_48_spatial_dz4_hi`). wCSET was higher at `{python} vieeg_48_winrate_min`–`{python} vieeg_48_winrate_max`% of timepoints. The AUC led to the same conclusion (largest p_corrected `{python} vieeg_48_auc_p4_max`, dz = `{python} vieeg_48_auc_dz4_lo`–`{python} vieeg_48_auc_dz4_hi`). Against GBF (median ρ = `{python} vieeg_48_r_beltrami`), neither metric differed significantly (rank correlation p_corrected `{python} vieeg_48_spatial_p_beltrami`, AUC p_corrected `{python} vieeg_48_auc_p_beltrami`), and wCSET was higher at `{python} vieeg_48_beltrami_winrate`% of timepoints.

Subject 2 did not reproduce this pattern: wCSET did not differ significantly from any other method on either metric (smallest p_corrected `{python} vieeg_34_p_min`). Median ρ was `{python} vieeg_34_r_wcset` for wCSET and `{python} vieeg_34_r_std_lo` to `{python} vieeg_34_r_std_hi` for the four other methods.

For comparison with @grova_intracranial_2016 and @afnan_assessing_2026, who report the signed Pearson correlation across contacts, we also computed that measure (Annex Figure 12). In Subject 1, it separated wCSET (median r = `{python} signed_48_wcset`) from sLORETA, dSPM, wMNE and CSET (`{python} signed_48_std_lo` to `{python} signed_48_std_hi`) more clearly than the polarity-invariant measures did (dz = `{python} signed_48_dz_lo`–`{python} signed_48_dz_hi`, largest p_corrected `{python} signed_48_p_max`). In Subject 2, it again showed no significant difference (smallest p_corrected `{python} signed_34_p_min`).


```{python filename="results_intra_vieeg_significance_plot.py"}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-intracranial-diff
#| fig-cap: "*Spatial agreement between virtual and recorded iEEG.* The two subjects with superficial sources (columns a, b); the two with deep sources are in Annex Figure 11. (a1, b1) Amplitude rank correlation per method at each timepoint of the comparison window: Spearman ρ across contacts between recorded and virtual absolute amplitude (box = IQR, line = median, outliers hidden; dotted line = 0). (a2, b2) Paired difference, wCSET minus each method, one value per timepoint (violin = distribution, thick line = median, thin line = IQR); positive = wCSET better. (a3, b3) Same for the AUC on |amplitude|: how well the virtual amplitudes identify the recorded active contacts (≥ 30% of the recorded maximum; 0.5 = chance). Above each violin: paired t-test with autocorrelation-corrected effective sample size (FDR-corrected), Cohen's dz, and the share of timepoints where wCSET is higher, minus 50% chance (e.g. +17% = higher at 67%)."
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

VIEEG_ORDER = ["wcset"] + COMPETITORS

# Main-text subjects only; 12 and 50 are in the Annex.
vieeg_fig, vieeg_axes = plt.subplots(
    3, len(MAIN_SUBJECTS), figsize=(4.6 * len(MAIN_SUBJECTS), 12),
    gridspec_kw={"hspace": 0.6, "wspace": 0.3}, squeeze=False,
)
for col_i, subject in enumerate(MAIN_SUBJECTS):
    letter = "ab"[col_i]

    # (1) Spatial correlation per method, chance range shaded
    ax = vieeg_axes[0, col_i]
    vieeg_metrics.plot.group_comparison(
        vieeg_results[(subject, _r)], order=VIEEG_ORDER, palette=COLORS, points=False, showfliers=False, width=0.55,
        alpha=0, saturation=1, fill_alpha=FILL_ALPHA, chance_value=0,
        tick_labels=METHOD_LABELS, reference_suffix=" (ref.)", ax=ax,
    )
    plt.setp(ax.get_xticklabels(), rotation=45, ha="right", fontsize=8)
    ax.set_xlabel("")
    ax.set_ylabel("Amplitude rank correlation (ρ)\nvirtual vs. recorded iEEG" if col_i == 0 else "", fontsize=8)
    ax.set_title(f"{letter}1. {SUBJECT_TITLES[subject]}: amplitude rank correlation per method", loc="left", fontsize=9)
    ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)

    # (2, 3) Paired differences per timepoint, positive = wCSET better
    for row_i, metric in enumerate(VIEEG_METRICS, start=1):
        dax = vieeg_axes[row_i, col_i]
        vieeg_metrics.plot.paired_differences(
            vieeg_results[(subject, metric)], reference="wcset", order=COMPETITORS, palette=COLORS,
            annotate=("stars", "effect", "winrate"), tick_labels=METHOD_LABELS, ax=dax,
            direction_labels=("wCSET better", "other method better") if col_i == len(MAIN_SUBJECTS) - 1 else None,
        )
        plt.setp(dax.get_xticklabels(), rotation=45, ha="right", fontsize=8)
        dax.set_title(f"{letter}{row_i + 1}. {SUBJECT_TITLES[subject]}: {VIEEG_METRICS[metric]},\n"
                      "paired difference vs. wCSET", loc="left", fontsize=9)
        if col_i == 0:
            dax.set_ylabel(f"wCSET − method\n({VIEEG_METRICS[metric]})", fontsize=8)
share_ylim(vieeg_axes[0])  # per-method row comparable across subjects
```

@fig-intra-reconstruction shows one timepoint in detail: the peak of the virtual iEEG's global field power (GFP), averaged over the two methods. In Subject 2, wCSET's largest amplitudes fell on the electrode shaft that dominated the recording, sharing `{python} glass_34_top_wcset` of its `{python} glass_n_top` strongest contacts, against `{python} glass_34_top_sloreta` for sLORETA (ρ = `{python} glass_34_rho_wcset` and `{python} glass_34_rho_sloreta`).

# Discussion

## Summary of Findings

We hypothesized that connectivity-informed methods would localize a source at its onset about as well as standard methods, but reconstruct the co-activation that follows more accurately (@sec-introduction). Our results support both parts of this hypothesis. In simulation (Study I) and in patients who underwent epilepsy surgery (Study II), wCSET localized the onset about as well as the standard methods. In simulation, it also reconstructed the subsequent co-activation markedly better, and simultaneous intracranial recordings (Study III) confirmed this advantage in one of the two patients analyzed, which offers preliminary support in real data.

The specific connectome mattered less than expected. In simulation, wCSET performed slightly better with surrogate connectomes that require no diffusion MRI than with the individual connectome used to generate the data, although it outperformed the standard methods with either. GBF, which uses cortical geometry instead of a connectome, performed on par with wCSET using the atlas surrogate. We discuss what these results imply for the role of the connectome in @sec-connectome-geometry.

These results also show that localization alone is an incomplete benchmark for source reconstruction. Localization did not consistently favor wCSET over the standard methods in either Study I or Study II, whereas measures of the spatial pattern of activity did, in simulation and in one intracranial patient. No single benchmark is sufficient. Simulations are exact but rest on simplified models of the head, of the spread of activity and of noise. Resections are clinically grounded but spatially coarse, and intracranial recordings are direct but sparse. Because each benchmark has a different blind spot, results that agree across them carry more weight than any one of them alone.

## Localization at Onset

At 25% of the rising phase, wCSET localized the simulated onset about as accurately as CSET and dSPM, and more accurately than sLORETA and wMNE. The differences from CSET and dSPM were significant, but only because of the large number of regions compared (`{python} simf_n_regions`). Their effects were small (r ≈ `{python} loc1_small_r`), so the three methods localized comparably. We expected this, because at onset, activity is still confined to the initial patch and has not yet reached any connected region. A prior that encodes connections between regions therefore has little to add.

Study II gave the same picture in patients. wCSET and GBF had the lowest localization errors, nearly identical to each other, and wCSET's maximum fell inside the resection volume in `{python} resection_inside_wcset` of `{python} resection_n` patients, against `{python} resection_inside_sloreta` for sLORETA. No difference between methods was significant, although every effect against the standard methods favored wCSET (r = `{python} resection_r_lo`–`{python} resection_r_hi`). With `{python} resection_n` patients, Study II could detect large differences in localization error, but not differences as small as those found in simulation. Since none was significant, its results confirm that localization differences between methods are small.

On the same cohort, @wang_geometry_2026 report a similar parity for GBF against dSPM, sLORETA and eLORETA (p = 0.079–0.133). They also report that GBF improved significantly over depth-weighted MNE (p = 0.012), the equivalent of our wMNE. Neither GBF nor wCSET did so in our analysis, possibly because our wMNE uses a different depth weighting and regularization (@sec-inverse).

In patients, however, localization was less accurate than in simulation. In simulation, wCSET's maximum lay a median of `{python} simf_loc_trial_median_wcset` mm from the initial patch. A resection volume is a much larger target than an initial patch, so we expected wCSET's maximum to fall inside it in nearly every patient. Yet it fell inside in only `{python} resection_inside_wcset` of `{python} resection_n`. Several differences between real recordings and our simulation may explain this gap. Real physiological noise is probably larger than our noise model assumes, and Study II could be whitened only with a diagonal noise covariance (@sec-data-resection). The target itself may also be imperfect. Interictal spikes arise from the irritative zone, which can extend beyond the epileptogenic zone and therefore beyond the resection [@rosenow_presurgical_2001]. Moreover, by 50% of the rising phase, the spike may already include activity that has propagated from its origin. 

Study II still answered the question it was included for. Localization against a resection is the field's conventional benchmark, and wCSET's advantage in reconstructing co-activation did not come at a cost in localization accuracy.

## Co-Activation

In simulation, wCSET's advantage appeared once activity had spread from the initial patch to connected regions, that is, once there was co-activation for a connectivity prior to capture. From onset until `{python} corr1_window_end_lo`–`{python} corr1_window_end_hi` ms, wCSET's spatial correlation with the ground truth was higher than that of every other method, and its advantage over the standard methods was largest close to the spike peak.

The connectome spectrum helps explain this timing. It describes activity as a combination of connectome harmonics, from low-frequency patterns that vary smoothly across connected regions to high-frequency patterns that vary rapidly (@sec-connectome). In visual evoked responses, @rue-queralt_connectome_2021 found that this spectrum became more compact as the response rose, meaning that a few harmonics, mostly of low frequency, captured most of the signal. wCSET's advantage rose with the simulated spike in the same way. Both connectome-based priors are built for such compact spectra. CSET's sparse prior favors a few harmonics, and wCSET's weights additionally favor the low-frequency ones. wCSET is therefore well suited to the moments when the signal has a compact connectome spectrum, such as when activity propagates across connected regions.

This advantage was robust. wCSET's spatial correlation remained higher than that of the standard methods down to an SNR of `{python} noise_corr_end_std`. It also withstood errors in the connectome, which matters because real tractography contains many false-positive connections [@maier-hein_challenge_2017]. Under perturbation of the connectome, wCSET's spatial correlation never became significantly lower than sLORETA's, whereas CSET's fell below sLORETA's once `{python} deg_loc_cset_worse_start`% of edges were swapped. With all edges swapped, the connectome no longer indicates which regions are connected, so wCSET can at best perform like a method without connectivity information. Even then, it did not perform worse.

Simultaneous intracranial recordings provide the most direct test of this advantage in real data, although with two patients analyzed, they offer a proof of concept rather than a validation (two further patients with deep sources are discussed in @sec-limitations). We compared virtual and recorded iEEG with two measures that ignore polarity, the Spearman correlation of absolute amplitudes and the AUC (@sec-metric-corr, @sec-metric-auc). The signed Pearson correlation used by @grova_intracranial_2016 and @afnan_assessing_2026 led to the same conclusions, with larger effects (@fig-annex-signed).

Over the whole comparison window, wCSET outperformed sLORETA, dSPM, wMNE and CSET on both measures in Patient 1, and did not differ from any of them in Patient 2. GBF performed on par with wCSET in both patients, and wCSET was never significantly worse than another method. @fig-intra-reconstruction shows a single time point, the peak of the virtual GFP, at which wCSET agreed better with the recording than sLORETA in both patients. In Patient 1, both methods placed their largest amplitudes on the correct electrode shafts, but mostly not on the correct contacts. In Patient 2, wCSET's largest amplitudes fell on the shaft that dominated the recording. This agreement did not persist over the rest of the window, which explains why the methods did not differ overall in that patient.

In Patients 1 and 2, absolute agreement with the recording was modest. On the signed correlation, wCSET's median over the comparison window was `{python} signed_48_wcset` in Patient 1 and `{python} signed_34_wcset` in Patient 2, within the 0.14–0.45 range that @afnan_assessing_2026 report between MEG and simultaneous SEEG at the spike peak. Agreement of this size thus seems inherent to this benchmark rather than specific to EEG or to our methods. Sparse sampling likely contributes. Even with 67 to 146 contacts per patient, the electrodes sample only a small fraction of the cortex on which activity is reconstructed.

Within these limits, the intracranial recordings support the simulation results. wCSET reconstructed the recorded activity better than the standard methods in Patient 1, and in neither patient was it worse than any other method

## Connectome or Geometry? {#sec-connectome-geometry}

wCSET did not need the individual connectome. In simulation, wCSET with the atlas or local surrogate, and GBF, which uses geometric harmonics instead of connectome harmonics, all outperformed wCSET with the individual connectome, both for localization (r = `{python} loc_wcset_r_lo`–`{python} loc_wcset_r_hi`) and, more strongly, for spatial correlation at the peak (r = `{python} corr_wcset_r_lo_pp`–`{python} corr_wcset_r_hi_pp`). This held even though the simulated activity spread along the individual connectome itself. No surrogate stood out, and binarized surrogates, in which all edges have the same weight, performed like weighted ones. In real data, where both methods relied on surrogates, a geometric surrogate did as well as a connectome surrogate. GBF and wCSET with the atlas connectome had the lowest median distances to the resection volume in Study II, and neither was significantly better than the other in either patient of Study III. @siu_structural_2026, who filtered source reconstructions with harmonics rather than using them as a prior, found the same parity between geometric and connectome harmonics against resected epileptogenic zones in 20 patients.

Why would surrogates outperform the very connectome on which the activity was simulated? We hypothesize that the answer lies in how spatially concentrated each graph's low-frequency harmonics are. To explore this, we computed the inverse participation ratio of the 200 lowest-frequency harmonics of each graph, a measure that is high when a harmonic is concentrated on few dipoles (@fig-annex-ipr). The individual connectome's harmonics often concentrated on small, sometimes disjoint groups of dipoles, whereas the surrogates' harmonics spread more evenly across the cortex. Because wCSET's weights favor low-frequency harmonics, a concentrated one pulls the reconstruction toward its cluster. Whether that cluster is actually active, however, depends on what the brain is doing at that moment. If it is not, the prior still pulls the reconstruction toward it, and the harmonic becomes a liability.

CSET's sparse prior should be less exposed to this problem. It selects only the few harmonics that best explain the data, so it can leave out a concentrated harmonic that does not match the activity, and it has little to gain from more homogeneous ones. Consistent with this, CSET performed only slightly worse with most surrogates than with the individual connectome. The exception was geometric harmonics, with which CSET localized markedly worse (r = `{python} cset_beltrami_loc_r`). The leading geometric harmonics are smooth, global patterns, so the few that a sparse prior selects may not be enough to place a focal onset.

A useful graph therefore needs two properties. First, it must reflect how the cortex is organized. With all edges of the connectome swapped at random, wCSET performed no better than the standard methods (@sec-s1-prior-noise). Second, its low-frequency harmonics must be spatially homogeneous enough. The individual connectome met the first requirement but not the second, which would explain why surrogates improved on it. The atlas connectome and the cortical geometry meet both. In practice, this means that wCSET does not require individual diffusion MRI, which is rarely acquired in clinical epilepsy workups.

These results do not mean that individual connectome harmonics are misleading, but that wCSET does not yet extract all the information they carry. Its weights, like GBF's, depend only on each harmonic's frequency, not on the recorded data, so it favors a concentrated harmonic whether or not its cluster is active. Selecting harmonics from the data, as CSET does, avoids this problem but raises another. Choosing a few harmonics among thousands is difficult, and although CSET was less exposed to concentrated harmonics, it performed worse than wCSET overall. A prior could combine the strengths of both by selecting harmonics from the data, but only among the low-frequency ones. Until then, wCSET's fixed weighting remains the better trade-off.

## Limitations {#sec-limitations}

Our source model restricts dipoles to the cortex (@sec-source-space), so it cannot represent deep generators. In Study III, the two patients whose activity arose from deep structures could not be reconstructed well by any method (@fig-annex-deep), a limitation that @grova_intracranial_2016 also report. This is a missed opportunity, because tractography, the very data our prior draws on, also captures connections to and among deep structures. Including these structures is not straightforward, however. On the cortex, each source can be oriented perpendicular to the surface, but deep structures offer no such surface, so their sources need free orientations. A connection between two sources pointing in different directions has no clear meaning, so the connectome would have to encode orientation as well.

For all methods except CSET, we set the regularization parameter α from the SNR of each recording (@sec-lambda). To see how far this choice was from the best possible one, we reconstructed the Study III recordings over a range of α values and measured each reconstruction's agreement with the intracranial signal (@fig-annex-alpha). The value with the best agreement was up to an order of magnitude away from the SNR-based value. In practice, however, no intracranial recording is available to find it. The two usual alternatives that need no reference, the L-curve and generalized cross-validation, gave implausible values on our data, so the SNR rule remained the best available choice. Choosing α without a reference therefore remains an open problem for source imaging in general. CSET's α was instead fixed after tuning in simulation, because no comparable rule exists for sparse priors, and this may have disadvantaged it in real data.

Our standard methods were limited to those available in MNE-Python. This excludes LORETA and LAURA, which @carboni_linear_2022 found most accurate for localizing interictal spikes, ahead of sLORETA and eLORETA.

Finally, only two patients could be evaluated in Study III. The test within each patient accounts for autocorrelation across time points, but two patients do not allow a test across patients, and more are needed before these results can be generalized.


# Conclusion

Source reconstruction methods are usually judged by how well they localize a single focal generator. Brain activity, however, rarely stays focal. It spreads to connected regions, and a method that localizes its onset well can still misrepresent the activity that follows. We therefore evaluated source reconstruction on both. We introduced wCSET, which replaces CSET's sparse prior with a Gaussian prior whose weights decay exponentially with graph frequency, and compared it with CSET, three standard methods and GBF in three settings: a simulation of activity spreading along the structural connectome, the resection volumes of seizure-free patients, and simultaneous intracranial recordings.

wCSET localized the onset of activity about as well as the standard methods, both in simulation and in the epilepsy surgery data. It reconstructed the co-activation that followed markedly better in simulation, and better against intracranial recordings in one of two patients, without ever performing significantly worse than another method. This advantage held under noise and substantial errors in the connectome. In simulation, connectome surrogates built without diffusion MRI even improved wCSET, so the method does not require individual diffusion MRI.

These results show that localization alone is an incomplete benchmark. The standard methods localized the onset well but reconstructed the co-activation that followed less accurately. Since activity rarely remains confined to one generator, how a method reconstructs distributed activity deserves as much weight as where it places the peak. The simulation of activity spreading along the connectome and the comparison with simultaneous intracranial recordings offer two ways to measure this, and both can be applied to any source reconstruction method. Extending connectivity-informed methods to deep generators is a natural next step. Together, these directions lead toward source reconstruction that reflects the brain's network organization rather than reducing it to a single point.

# Conclusion

Source reconstruction is usually benchmarked on how well it localizes a single focal generator, which says little about how well a method captures the co-activation of distributed regions. We introduced wCSET, which replaces CSET's sparse prior with a Gaussian prior whose weights decay exponentially with graph frequency. We evaluated it against CSET, three standard methods and a geometric alternative (GBF) in three settings: a simulation of activity spreading along the structural connectome, the resection volumes of seizure-free patients, and simultaneous intracranial recordings.

wCSET localized the onset of activity about as well as the standard methods, both in simulation and in the epilepsy surgery data. It reconstructed the co-activation that followed markedly better in simulation, and better against intracranial recordings in one of two patients, without ever performing significantly worse than another method. This advantage held under noise and substantial errors in the connectome. In simulation, connectome surrogates built without diffusion MRI even improved wCSET, so the method does not require individual diffusion MRI. GBF performed on par with wCSET in all three studies, as two independent groups also report [@wang_geometry_2026; @siu_structural_2026]. A useful connectome therefore needs to be anatomically plausible, with harmonics that spread evenly over the cortex, but it does not need to be individually exact. Priors that select harmonics from the data could make better use of individual connectomes.

Beyond wCSET itself, we see the evaluation framework as a lasting contribution. Together, its three parts test a method on the full pattern of activity rather than on its onset alone. Two of them are new to source imaging and can be used on their own. The first is a simulation in which activity spreads along the structural connectome in dipole space. The second uses simultaneous EEG–iEEG recordings to test reconstruction beyond localization. The natural next steps are to apply this framework to future connectivity- and geometry-informed methods, and to extend it to source models that include deep generators. Both lead toward source reconstruction that reflects the brain's network organization rather than reducing it to a single point.
